used_additions.where: When should someone see a GP?
used_additions.sentence: If your joints are sore with a high or low temperature, or the skin around a joint is red or hot, the NHS says to ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111.
used_additions.evidence: NHS arthritis page: urgent GP or NHS 111 for red/hot skin or sore joints with temperature

used_additions.sentence: No single blood test can prove or rule out rheumatoid arthritis, so doctors combine blood tests, scans and an examination.
used_additions.evidence: NHS diagnosis: no blood test can definitively prove or rule out RA

used_additions.sentence: Osteoarthritis does not usually need X-rays or blood tests, but they may be used to rule out other causes such as rheumatoid arthritis.
used_additions.evidence: NHS: further tests not usually necessary but may rule out other causes

used_additions.sentence: If rheumatoid arthritis is suspected, the GP may do blood tests and refer you to a specialist.
used_additions.evidence: NHS/NRAS: GP may start with blood tests and refer to a specialist

used_additions.sentence: There is no cure for osteoarthritis, but treatment can help with symptoms.
used_additions.evidence: NHS treatment page: no cure, but does not necessarily get worse

used_additions.sentence: Rheumatoid arthritis can also cause firm lumps called rheumatoid nodules under the skin.
used_additions.evidence: NHS RA: rheumatoid nodules can develop under the skin

used_additions.sentence: Hot or cold packs can ease osteoarthritis symptoms.
used_additions.evidence: NHS treatment: hot or cold packs can ease symptoms
